## Solution-Specific Details

### Ceph RGW

Ceph's RADOS Gateway provides the most comprehensive S3 API implementation among open-source solutions. Maximum object size is 5TB, with a 5GB limit on single PUT operations. Supports both Signature v2 and v4. Multi-site replication uses a Realm/Zonegroup/Zone hierarchy with active-active support (default since the Kraken release), though async replication is not recommended for single stretched clusters over WAN [26].

### MinIO

MinIO implements extensive S3 API coverage including all core operations, multipart upload, versioning, lifecycle management, encryption, and object lock. Notable omissions: ACLs are not supported (policies are used instead), and website hosting, logging, and metrics endpoints are absent. AbortIncompleteMultipartUpload as a lifecycle action is not supported. Site replication provides active-active mesh synchronization of buckets, objects, and IAM, but requires matching IDP configurations, matching MinIO versions, and mandatory bucket versioning; it is mutually exclusive with bucket-level replication [58].

### SeaweedFS

SeaweedFS provides near-complete S3 API coverage [13]. Supported features include ACLs, CORS, encryption (SSE-KMS, SSE-C, SSE-S3), lifecycle (expiration actions only — transitions not supported), versioning, object lock, bucket policies, object tagging, and STS/IAM APIs. S3 Tables (Iceberg) support is also present [13].

Unsupported: cross-region replication, event notifications, and website hosting [13].

Behavioral differences from AWS S3: SeaweedFS uses real directories (not key prefixes), and DeleteObject on a prefix key deletes the entire folder [13].

### Cloudflare R2

R2 has the most limited S3 feature set among the evaluated solutions [7]. Supported operations cover basic bucket and object CRUD, multipart upload, and SSE-C encryption. Region is always "auto" and cannot be specified [7].

Unsupported: versioning, ACLs, bucket policies, object tagging, object lock, SSE-KMS, SSE-S3, cross-region replication, website hosting, and event notifications [7].

Risk: UploadPart replacement behavior differs from AWS S3 — uploading a part with the same part number may not replace the previous part, creating potential data integrity issues [7].

### Garage

Garage returns HTTP 501 for unimplemented S3 endpoints, making incompatibilities explicit rather than silently failing [12]. Supported operations include core bucket/object operations, multipart upload, SSE-C encryption, and partial lifecycle management (expiration and abort incomplete multipart only) [12]. Website hosting is partially supported (no redirect rules) [12].

Unsupported: versioning, ACLs, bucket policies, object tagging, object lock, SSE-S3/SSE-KMS, cross-region replication, and event notifications [12]. Only Signature v4 is supported [12].

### Wasabi

Wasabi claims near-complete S3 compatibility. S3 Select is the only documented unsupported feature. Object Lock is supported with both bucket-level Compliance mode and object-level locking, assessed by Cohasset Associates for SEC 17a-4/CFTC/FINRA compliance [60]. Unlocking compliance-locked objects requires contacting Wasabi Customer Support [60].

### Backblaze B2

B2's S3 compatibility is limited [9]. Encryption supports SSE-B2 (Backblaze-managed) and SSE-C, but not SSE-KMS or SSE-S3 [9]. Bucket ACLs are a simple toggle between private and public-read with no per-object ACLs [9]. Object tagging API calls succeed but return empty results [9]. No support for IAM roles, website hosting, or POST-based uploads [9]. Only Signature v4 is supported [9].

### NetApp StorageGRID

StorageGRID implements "most operations" of the S3 REST API with custom extensions for platform-specific features [44]. S3 clients connect through Gateway Nodes or Admin Nodes [44].

### Dell ECS

ECS implements a "subset" of the S3 API. Lifecycle management is limited to expiration actions only. Versioning has implementation quirks that differ from AWS S3 behavior. Federation supports up to 8 VDCs with continuous async replication [69].

### Scality ARTESCA / RING

Scality claims high S3 compatibility including versioning, object lock, lifecycle management, and encryption with "100% AWS-compatible" positioning. RING extends into NFS and FUSE protocols alongside S3 [85].

### VAST Data

S3 capabilities include object versioning, object lock (added in v4.3), multipart uploads, and IAM [49]. VAST provides multi-protocol access (S3, NFS, SMB) to the same data [49].

### IBM Cloud Object Storage

IBM COS implements the "most commonly used subset" of S3 operations with HMAC authentication and IBM-specific API extensions [84].

## The Compatibility Spectrum

S3 "compatibility" is not a binary attribute. Key distinctions:

1. **Data-plane vs. management-plane operations** — Most solutions implement data operations (GET, PUT, DELETE, multipart) reliably. Management-plane operations (lifecycle, replication, notifications, IAM) are where implementations diverge significantly.

2. **Behavioral fidelity** — Even "supported" operations may behave differently. SeaweedFS uses real directories instead of flat key namespaces [13]. R2's UploadPart replacement semantics differ from AWS [7]. ECS versioning has quirks. Backblaze B2 tagging returns empty sets rather than errors [9].

3. **No industry-standard certification** — There is no formal S3 compatibility certification or test suite. Claims of "100% compatible" are self-asserted and untestable without running application-specific workloads against the target platform.

4. **Lifecycle feature depth** — "Lifecycle support" ranges from full AWS parity (expiration, transitions between storage classes, abort incomplete multipart, intelligent tiering) to expiration-only (SeaweedFS [13], ECS, Garage [12]).

5. **Error handling** — Solutions handle unsupported operations differently. Garage returns 501 (Not Implemented) [12], making gaps explicit. Others may return 200 with no-op behavior (B2 tagging [9]) or undocumented errors.

## Gaps and Limitations

1. **Self-reported data** — Compatibility claims come from vendor documentation, not independent testing. No solution was validated by running a standard S3 test suite during this research.
2. **Ceph RGW detail** — While Ceph RGW is described as comprehensive, the specific citation for feature-by-feature coverage came from discovery agent analysis rather than a single canonical compatibility matrix document.
3. **Scality specifics** — The "100% AWS-compatible" claim was extracted from marketing materials rather than technical documentation listing supported and unsupported operations.
4. **Dell ECS versioning quirks** — The nature of ECS versioning differences from AWS S3 was noted but not detailed in the sources collected.
5. **Wasabi verification** — Wasabi's "100% bit-compatible" claim and the S3 Select exception came from discovery agent findings rather than primary Wasabi documentation visited in-session.
6. **MinIO post-archive status** — MinIO's API compatibility was documented while the project was active. The archived codebase remains usable, but no further API additions or fixes will occur [5].
7. **Data loss risks** — Ceph RGW has a documented `--bypass-gc` flag that can cause data loss. MinIO's tiering feature can cause data loss when the scanner cannot repair metadata of transitioned objects [61]. These operational risks are separate from API compatibility but affect real-world reliability.
